title: Recall elections: who replaces a removed official?

shots.narration: A recall lets voters remove an elected official before the term ends. Proposition five changes what happens next. It does not eliminate the power to recall state officials.
shots.headline: Removal and replacement are different decisions

shots.narration: Today, a state recall ballot normally asks two questions: whether to remove the official, and who should replace them. If removal wins, the replacement candidate with the most votes takes office.
shots.headline: Today: two questions on one ballot

shots.narration: Proposition five removes the replacement question. The office would be filled through succession, appointment, or a separate election, depending on the office and when the recall happens.
shots.headline: Proposed: one recall question

shots.narration: Imagine opening a ballot during a recall election.
shots.headline: What would you be asked?

shots.narration: In a hypothetical crowded replacement contest, one candidate could lead with thirty votes out of a hundred. Winning the most votes is different from winning a majority. That is one concern motivating the change.
shots.headline: Most votes need not mean a majority

shots.narration: Election staff would explain a different replacement process.
shots.headline: The next step depends on the office

shots.narration: If a legislator is recalled, a special election would generally fill the seat. Vacancies in most other state offices would be filled by gubernatorial appointment. So a separate replacement vote is not guaranteed for every office.
shots.headline: Different offices, different routes

shots.narration: For the governor, the lieutenant governor would take over. If the recall happens early enough, before the specified nomination deadline in the first two years, voters elect a new governor at a later statewide election. Otherwise, the lieutenant governor completes the term.
shots.headline: The governor has a timing rule

shots.narration: Costs could rise if an additional special election is needed, or fall when replacement-candidate materials disappear. The analyst says the net effect is unknown, with possible costs or savings of millions per recall.
shots.headline: Election costs can move either way
items: Net effect depends on future recalls

shots.narration: A voter might want removal considered on its own, rather than as a shortcut for a candidate with limited support. Familiar vacancy procedures could make succession more predictable. That does not mean every replacement would be elected in a new majority vote.
shots.headline: The case for YES
items: Separate removal from a crowded replacement race

shots.narration: You might want to choose the replacement yourself, immediately.
shots.headline: Your question: who gets to choose?

shots.narration: Another voter could object to giving appointments or automatic succession a larger role. They may prefer seeing the alternatives on the same ballot, and worry that a later election leaves them waiting. These are choices about accountability, not just administrative convenience.
shots.headline: The case for NO

shots.narration: In the September PPIC survey of likely voters, 35 percent said yes, 59 percent no, and 5 percent were unsure. These are dated survey results, not votes already cast.
shots.headline: September snapshot: PPIC

shots.narration: Yes changes the replacement process; no keeps the replacement question on recall ballots. Visit our website for the fuller explanation, source links, and official voter guide. Compare the tradeoffs, then make your own informed choice.
shots.headline: Explore the full explanation

Official voter guide, measure text and attributed campaign arguments.
September likely-voter results, original published values retained including rounding.

polling_note: Selected verified surveys available at the October 19 research check; dates shown explicitly. Not a polling average or forecast. Rounded percentages may total 99 or 101. Other polls may differ.
editorial_note: Illustrative characters and calculations are not real testimonials or guaranteed outcomes. Voter considerations describe reasons for either choice, not recommendations.
